posts.author: elonmusk
posts.text:
In 2018, Elon Musk tweeted that he would fund the replacement of lead contaminated water pipes in Flint, Michigan for any home that still had unsafe water. He said to just tell him which houses needed help and he would fix them. The response from Flint's officials was near silence.

The offer was genuine. Elon followed up. He donated $480,000 to install UV filtration systems in Flint schools. He offered to continue funding until every household had clean water. Local officials thanked him publicly and then largely stopped responding. The project stalled not because of money but because of bureaucracy, local politics, and the same institutional inertia that had allowed the crisis to happen in the first place.

The detail that makes this story devastating is not the donation. It is the disconnect between the speed at which Elon operates and the speed at which a municipal government can accept help. He offered. He funded. He followed up. The system he was trying to help could not process the help at the speed it was offered. The man who can build a factory in 6 months could not get a city to accept pipe replacements because the approval process, the contractor bids, the environmental reviews, and the political negotiations moved at a pace that made SpaceX look like light speed by comparison.

He has described the Flint experience as one of the most frustrating of his career. Not because the problem was hard. Because the problem was easy and the system designed to solve easy problems was broken. The water needed clean pipes. The pipes needed money. The money was offered. And the space between offered and installed was filled with a bureaucracy that moved at the speed of government while children drank contaminated water.

The man who solves engineering problems for a living encountered a problem that was not engineering. It was institutional. The pipes were simple. The politics were not. The money was present. The will was present. The system that was supposed to connect money and will to pipes could not function at the speed the crisis demanded.

He fixed the schools. The broader offer faded. The city eventually replaced most of its pipes through federal and state funding years later. The man who offered to fix it in months watched it take years. The frustration of the man who moves fast encountering a world that doesn't is the frustration that defines his relationship with every institution he touches. The rockets are faster because they don't require a city council vote.

posts.text:
Bill Ackman says Neuralink and other brain-computer interfaces will let the blind see again within "not too many years"

“And you know, my daughter, who lost pretty much basic function, ability to walk, ability to speak, ability to see, is regaining function. She’s cognitively, as far as I can tell, fine. She’s relearning how to speak, and she’s learning again how to walk. And I’m confident we’re going to get her back."

"Biggest challenge right now is that the optic nerve damage from the pressure on the brain has caused her to lose probably 98% of her vision."

"But even there I’m optimistic. Spent a lot of time in the last few months meeting with all these brain computer interface companies, obviously Neuralink being the most famous, but there’s some other very promising lower intervention technologies."

"And this will be a period, you know, AI is going to enable us. We’re going to be able to get more signal from the brain, and we’re going to be able to interpret that signal much more effectively than we had before. And the blind will see again, and people who have not been able to walk, so to speak, paraplegics, I believe will walk again. It’s a matter of not months but years, but not too many years.”

quote.author: firesidealpha
quote.name: Fireside Alpha
quote.text:
Bill Ackman says Elon Musk might have to borrow a trillion dollars to open gigawatts of data centers, keeping rates persistently high, and that neoclouds are like levered real estate developers sensitive to the cost of capital

“So, I think it is sustainable because, you know, intelligence is again an enormously valuable asset. And I think the demand therefore for the compute that enables intelligence, I think, is going to be sustained."

"And, you know, the companies that are, you know, the hyperscalers that are building out a lot of this infrastructure have the financial resources, the creditworthiness in order to access the capital."

"I worry more about the pure play neocloud companies that are a bit like highly levered real estate developers playing a theme. I think they’re much more at risk. They’re much more sensitive to the cost of capital."

"But you have, I mean, SpaceX, Elon on the earnings call gave some projections for how many gigawatts of data centers he was going to open. If he meets his objective, he might have to borrow a trillion dollars of capital."

"So, you have companies competing at sovereign levels for debt. And the result is, you know, this massive, you know, more and more supply of debt. So, I don’t see a world in which, you know, there’s a dramatic, you know, there’s a lot of demand for capital and a finite supply. So, I think that makes rates persistently high.”

quote.author: lumenxbt
quote.name: Lumen
quote.text:
Ten million people have watched a comedian accidentally destroy the entire TED talk industry.

He filmed the talk once at TEDxNewYork in 2014 and openly admitted he had nothing to say.

Speaking coaches charge $5,000 to teach the exact tricks he used in 6 minutes to say nothing at all.

His name is Will Stephen. He is a comedian from Late Night with Seth Meyers who was invited to give a real TED talk and used it to prove the format is a costume anyone can wear.

Every TED speaker opens with a question, tells a personal story, cites a scientist, and shows a chart. Stephen did all four in six minutes with zero content.

His entire formula fits on a napkin.

Gesture with both hands. Ask the audience a question anyone can answer. Tell a mildly embarrassing story so they say aww. Point to a stranger on a slide and call them important. Flash a chart of random numbers. Wear glasses with no lenses. The audience will think you are brilliant.

That last trick alone has probably cost the public speaking coaching industry a hundred million dollars in sessions clients should have skipped.

"If you watched me on YouTube with the sound off, you would think I was a genius."

That is Will Stephen on the TED stage, three minutes into the talk he was paid to give. He wasn't lying.

Executives pay $15,000 for a keynote coach and still open with a joke the room never laughs at. Founders rehearse their pitch for weeks and still sound like Stephen at minute four, saying "wagga wah, gabba gabba" with authority.

The talk is free on YouTube. The method is written across every TED speaker's playbook for ten years.

Stephen still writes for Seth Meyers. Almost none of the ten million viewers have stopped nodding at empty slides since.

The formula is free. The willingness to actually say something before your next keynote, pitch, or townhall is the entire edge.

AUSTIN MAN slams into a stopped minivan at 103 mph on Mother's Day, right in front of a cop, and kills a fire captain hours after his fifth son was born. DA Jose Garza's office asked him to pay a small fine.

Marvin Taylor was on his way to pick up his four other boys so they could meet their new baby brother. He was sitting at a red light on Koenig Lane when a Dodge Durango doing 103 in a 45 zone slammed into him and threw his van 150 feet. He died pinned inside.

The officer found the driver, Rodney Bremby, with bloodshot eyes and slurred speech and stench of alcohol. 

He was charged with intoxication manslaughter, which carries up to 20 years in prison. A judge revoked his bond twice while the case was pending, and both times he was back out within two weeks.

On Monday he got 10 years of probation, community service, and $535 in fees.

Five boys have lost their father, and the man who killed him just had to pay a small fine and promise not do it again before going back home.

The scale of Starlink is almost impossible to comprehend

Out of 16,848 active satellites in orbit as of October 31, 2026, 11,184 are Starlink

That's 66% of every active satellite humanity has in orbit

Just look at the numbers:

• Starlink: 11,184
• OneWeb: 651
• Amazon Kuiper: 391
• Qianfan (China): 257
• Iridium: 80

Starlink alone has nearly 2 TIMES more active satellites than every other operator on Earth COMBINED

And what's even more insane is how fast SpaceX built this

On May 24, 2019, Falcon 9 launched the first batch of 60 Starlink satellites

Just 2,717 days later, SpaceX is still launching batches of 27 satellites, including another mission on October 31

SpaceX has built the largest satellite constellation in human history, at a scale no other operator comes close to matching

And this is just the beginning
